query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: During intermediate temperature thermal aging or deformation, inherent chemical complexity triggers the nanoclustering of principal elements (such as Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries in single-phase HEAs, and once a critical density and size of these clusters are reached, they reduce intergranular cohesion sufficiently to cause brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi or refractory HEA such as Ti–V–Nb–Ta) with a homogeneous elemental distribution established during processing.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to isothermal thermal aging and intermediate-temperature deformation to promote atomic diffusion and nanocluster formation at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Intermediate service temperatures (typically 450–700°C) and moderate strain rates where atomic mobility is sufficient to drive nanocluster formation yet below the threshold for significant grain coarsening or extensive secondary phase precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale clusters of principal elements that form along grain boundaries as a result of thermal activation and diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under service-relevant conditions, the complex chemical environment in HEAs leads to the gradual aggregation of principal elements into nanoclusters specifically at grain boundaries. As these clusters grow in density and size, they locally degrade cohesion by disrupting the uniform bonding network, thereby facilitating premature intergranular fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: After intermediate temperature aging, samples will exhibit an increased density of nanoclusters at grain boundaries, accompanied by a significant reduction in ductility and fracture toughness relative to the as-processed state, as evidenced by mechanical testing and high-resolution microscopy.
generation.baseline: A single-phase HEA with a uniform distribution of principal elements and high toughness prior to any thermal aging or deformation-induced clustering.
generation.boundary: This nanoclustering mechanism is expected to dominate within a temperature range where atomic diffusion is active (approximately 450–700°C) but before other phase transformations or grain coarsening become the primary factors affecting mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall trend is conceptually supported, the exact critical cluster size, density, and time scales needed to transition from ductile to brittle behavior remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples and subject them to controlled thermal aging at intermediate temperatures. Use in situ TEM and atom probe tomography to monitor the kinetics of nanocluster formation at grain boundaries. Relate the evolution of cluster density and size with changes in mechanical properties through tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Nanocluster size, density, and chemical composition at grain boundaries over aging time
Tensile elongation, fracture toughness, and creep rupture life measurements
Fractographic analysis to confirm intergranular fracture correlating with nanocluster presence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant nanoclustering occurs without a corresponding degradation of intergranular cohesion and if the mechanical properties do not decline as predicted, then the hypothesis that nanoclustering is the principal cause of embrittlement is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). Taking the well-studied equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA as an example, this alloy is a single fcc-phase solid solution after homogenization at temperatures ≥1000°C for up to 2 days and recrystallization at temperatures ≥800°C for 1 hour (, ). Various intermetallic phases are precipitated primarily at GBs during annealing at intermediate temperatures for tens to hundreds of days in coarse-grained alloys (), while mere minutes in nanocrystalline alloy

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. Reinforced with specific processing parameters to generate serrated versus straight boundaries.

minor_issues: Exact critical cluster size and formation kinetics remain unclear and may be sensitive to subtle compositional and processing variations.
fixes: Provide quantitative modeling or measurement of cluster formation energy and kinetics to substantiate the proposed transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
evidence_needs: Comparative high-resolution microscopy studies (e.g., atom probe tomography) at different aging times and temperatures to confirm composition and evolution of boundary clusters.

major_issues: Largely replicates the same mechanism and experimental approach as candidate A without new or more detailed mechanistic justification.
fixes: Differentiate more clearly from candidate A by specifying additional driving forces for nanoclustering or unique experimental conditions that would yield new insights.
evidence_needs: Further thermodynamic or kinetic modeling to validate the role of chemical complexity in promoting boundary clustering beyond known segregation effects.

major_issues: Emphasis on high strain rate conditions does not closely match typical service environments for high-entropy alloys.
Lacks direct citation or prior evidence linking vacancy-induced nanocavity formation at grain boundaries to brittle fracture in these alloys.
fixes: Clarify whether this mechanism is relevant to routine engineering conditions or only to extreme loading scenarios.
Incorporate known data or computations quantifying vacancy generation and coalescence rates in HEAs at elevated temperatures.
evidence_needs: Experimental or computational studies confirming that vacancy clusters indeed form at high rates under relevant temperatures and that they cause intergranular embrittlement in single-phase HEAs.

minor_issues: Does not incorporate the influence of compositional complexity or possible segregation phenomena that could interact with boundary morphology.
fixes: Clarify whether morphological design alone can outweigh or interact with any element segregation effects under relevant service conditions.
evidence_needs: Comparative data isolating boundary morphology effects from compositional variations (consistent grain size, texture, and chemistry) to confirm that altered boundary geometry is the principal factor.

minor_issues: Uncertain whether typical impurity levels are sufficient to drive significant precipitate formation in all single-phase HEAs.
fixes: Quantify the thresholds for impurity content and aging duration that produce detectable boundary precipitates.
evidence_needs: Further studies on the precise role and solubility limits of common interstitials (O, N) in different HEA systems.
Comparative doping experiments to confirm that controlling impurities changes embrittlement and fracture modes.
